power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Caregivers who had at least one child between 3-5 years old residing in South Africa were recruited into the study in January 2026. Prospective participants received a study invitation link randomized to one of four conditions: access to BS-VT and prompted with reminder nudges, access to the BS-VT and prompted with goal-setting nudges, access to the BS-VT app alone, or given no access to the BS-VT app. These groups are henceforth referred to as the treatment groups (Reminder Nudges, Goal-Setting Nudges, BookSmart Alone, respectively), and the control group. 812 participants enrolled in the study and completed a baseline survey, see Figure 2. Attrition led to a final sample size of 519 participants (M age = 4.33 years, SD age = 0.80, range = 2.97-6.00) who completed both baseline and endline surveys, see Figure 2. Attrition did not differ between groups (F(3, 808) = 1.23, p = .299). Note that higher SES predicted endline survey completion (β = 0.61, SE = 0.14, t = 4.35, p < .001). Caregivers were recruited through MoyaApp, a free-to-download super app in South Africa that houses BS-VT as a mini app, enabling data-free access for families and addressing access in underserved communities for whom data costs are a significant barrier. See Supplementary Methods for details about MoyaApp and recruitment process. A power analysis (β = 0.9) determined that a sample of 634 participants was necessary to detect a small effect (MDES f = 0.15). The final sample of 519 corresponds to a MDES of 0.166. The study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework Note. Participants who enrolled in the study (enrolled sample), completed both baseline and endline measures (final sample), accessed BS-VT, and engaged with BS-VT. Despite our best attempts to block their access to the app, some participants in the control group (n = 48) still signed onto BookSmart throughout the intervention (n = 30 engaged with BookSmart content).

table.text: Caregivers who had at least one child between 3-5 years old residing in South Africa were recruited into the study in January 2026. Prospective participants received a study invitation link randomized to one of four conditions: access to BS-VT and prompted with reminder nudges, access to the BS-VT and prompted with goal-setting nudges, access to the BS-VT app alone, or given no access to the BS-VT app. These groups are henceforth referred to as the treatment groups (Reminder Nudges, Goal-Setting Nudges, BookSmart Alone, respectively), and the control group. 812 participants enrolled in the study and completed a baseline survey, see Figure 2. Attrition led to a final sample size of 519 participants (M age = 4.33 years, SD age = 0.80, range = 2.97-6.00) who completed both baseline and endline surveys, see Figure 2. Attrition did not differ between groups (F(3, 808) = 1.23, p = .299). Note that higher SES predicted endline survey completion (β = 0.61, SE = 0.14, t = 4.35, p < .001). Caregivers were recruited through MoyaApp, a free-to-download super app in South Africa that houses BS-VT as a mini app, enabling data-free access for families and addressing access in underserved communities for whom data costs are a significant barrier. See Supplementary Methods for details about MoyaApp and recruitment process. A power analysis (β = 0.9) determined that a sample of 634 participants was necessary to detect a small effect (MDES f = 0.15). The final sample of 519 corresponds to a MDES of 0.166. The study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework Note. Participants who enrolled in the study (enrolled sample), completed both baseline and endline measures (final sample), accessed BS-VT, and engaged with BS-VT. Despite our best attempts to block their access to the app, some participants in the control group (n = 48) still signed onto BookSmart throughout the intervention (n = 30 engaged with BookSmart content).

table.text: Providing caregivers with access to BS-VT produced limited impacts on caregiver and child outcomes, however, nudging caregivers to engage with BS-VT produced positive child outcomes, including stronger academic (early literacy and numeracy), cognitive, and language skills, specifically for more vulnerable children (i.e., children from lower-SES families and children with lower baseline skills)-albeit these effects were mostly marginally significant (p < .05 and q < .1) and did not meet our threshold for statistical significance (q < .05).

table.header: Discussion

table.text: Here, we found that children from lower SES households and children with low baseline scores showed positive impacts in social-emotional, cognitive, and language skills when caregivers received behavioral nudges, albeit these effects were largely marginally significant (q < .1).

table.formatted: Providing caregivers with access to BS-VT produced limited impacts on caregiver and child outcomes, however, nudging caregivers to engage with BS-VT produced positive child outcomes, including stronger academic (early literacy and numeracy), cognitive, and language skills, specifically for more vulnerable children (i.e., children from lower-SES families and children with lower baseline skills)-albeit these effects were mostly marginally significant (p < .05 and q < .1) and did not meet our threshold for statistical significance (q < .05).
table.header: Discussion
table.expanded: Providing caregivers with access to BS-VT produced limited impacts on caregiver and child outcomes, however, nudging caregivers to engage with BS-VT produced positive child outcomes, including stronger academic (early literacy and numeracy), cognitive, and language skills, specifically for more vulnerable children (i.e., children from lower-SES families and children with lower baseline skills)-albeit these effects were mostly marginally significant (p < .05 and q < .1) and did not meet our threshold for statistical significance (q < .05).

table.formatted: It's also important to note that several effects did not meet the threshold for statistical significance (q < .05), but were marginally significant (p < .05 and q < .1) and caution should be applied when interpreting these findings.
table.header: Limitations and Future Directions
table.expanded: It's also important to note that several effects did not meet the threshold for statistical significance (q < .05), but were marginally significant (p < .05 and q < .1) and caution should be applied when interpreting these findings.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p > .05", "p > .05"), Text = c("Insignificant values (p > .05) are blank.", 
"Insignificant values (p > .05) are left blank.")), row.names = c(NA, 
-2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 216 columns across 3 data files.
#### Issues Identified

6 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("Vroom Tip Type Data.xlsx", "Worldreader Data.xlsx", "Worldreader Data.xlsx", "Worldreader Data.xlsx", "Worldreader Data.xlsx", "Worldreader Data.xlsx"), Column = c("VroomTipType", "BookSmartSatisfaction_InDepth", "EdTechUsageIn3Months_Specify", "Family_AdultsInTheHome", "PriorEdTechUsage_Specify", "VroomTipsSatisfaction_InDepth"), Issues = c("🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Column name suggests personal information (matched: ip)", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 42 characters, 92% distinct) may contain n...", "🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: booksmart/Booksmart/bookSmart/Bo...", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 94% numeric but 25 values cannot be parsed: \"1 my fiancee...", "🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: youtube/YouTube", "🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: prefer not to say/Prefer not to say" )), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 3 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Participants were randomized into four groups: BS-VT with goal-setting nudges, BS-VT with reminder nudges, BS-VT (no behavioral nudges), and a wait-listed control group.
Caregivers who had at least one child between 3-5 years old residing in South Africa were recruited into the study in January 2026.

These groups are henceforth referred to as the treatment groups (Reminder Nudges, Goal-Setting Nudges, BookSmart Alone, respectively), and the control group. 812 participants enrolled in the study and completed a baseline survey, see Figure 2.

Caregivers were recruited through MoyaApp, a free-to-download super app in South Africa that houses BS-VT as a mini app, enabling data-free access for families and addressing access in underserved communities for whom data costs are a significant barrier.
2 Participants were typically compensated 90 rand.

Most in-depth interview studies achieve saturation with samples of 9-17 (Hennink & Kaiser, 2022), suggesting that our sample size should have provided sufficient results. 7 participants were caregivers of 3 year olds, 5 were caregivers of 4 year olds, and 8 were caregivers of 5 year olds.
Participants completed a baseline interview between November 3 and November 14, 2025.
After opening the baseline survey link, potential participants were required to pass two additional screening checkpoints to ensure we only captured responses from eligible participants.
If more than two comprehension questions were completed incorrectly, participants were deemed ineligible for the study.
First, from an ethical standpoint, it was essential to ensure that all participants were fully informed about the study before providing consent.

Use and engagement with BS-VT was operationalized as the number of books completed in BookSmart, the number of Vroom Tips TM completed, and as a dichotomous engagement variable: if a participant completed any books or Vroom Tips TM throughout the intervention, they were scored as "yes" for having engaged, otherwise participants were scored as "no".
Potential participants were first asked to select the age ranges of the children they care for.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 1 R code file.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
    Basis = "none"), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Missing inputs
1 input file the code reads is in the deposit but not usable as named: too large to download, inside an archive, or under a similar name.

```{r}

-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 1 script: 0 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 1 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "Worldreader Analyses.R", Outcome = "dependency_unavailable", 
    Detail = "dependency_unavailable", "Time (s)" = 2), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Dependency-unavailable errors**

**1 script could not run because its own dependency is unavailable** — the package failed to install from both live CRAN and the CRAN Archive (or a GitHub/URL source could not be resolved). This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper's code, so it does **not** force the traffic light red.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "Worldreader Analyses.R"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**1 script calls `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

```{r}
table <- structure(list(File = "Worldreader Analyses.R", "setwd() removed" = 1L,

), class = "data.frame")
```

text.text: This study is a mixed-methods impact evaluation of a digital parenting and shared book reading intervention (Worldreader's BookSmart app with embedded parenting tips, Vroom Tips TM ) on caregivers' self-efficacy, beliefs, and practices, and early childhood outcomes in South Africa.
We further investigated whether behavioral nudges could promote sustained engagement.

Study 1 consisted of a 4-arm randomized controlled trial (BookSmart, BookSmart with reminder nudges, BookSmart with goal-setting nudges, control group) where caregivers (N = 519) of children aged 3-5 years used BookSmart for 15 weeks.
We found randomization to access the intervention (i.e., intent-to-treat) had no significant effect on caregiver or child outcomes.

However, behavioral nudges, particularly goal-setting messages, increased caregiver engagement and improved cognitive and language skills specifically for disadvantaged children (i.e., children from lower-SES households and children with lower baseline skills).
Greater intervention engagement (i.e., treatment-on-the-treated) was significantly associated with language skills and marginally associated with literacy skills.
Study 2 consisted of qualitative interviews with caregivers (N = 20) before and after using BookSmart for 3 weeks.

Results indicated that several barriers impacted caregivers' engagement with the intervention, including costs (e.g., airtime) and language accessibility (e.g., caregivers reported translating English books into their native language).

Our results highlight that digital reading interventions have the potential to support early childhood development, while stressing that engagement with the intervention is critical in realizing potential positive outcomes.
The findings suggest that access and usage barriers should be considered when designing interventions and that behavioral nudges may serve to increase engagement.

Around 250 million children globally under the age of 5 are at risk of poor developmental outcomes, including social-emotional and cognitive skills foundational to learning and academic success (Lu et al., 2016).

text.text: This issue disproportionately affects low-and middle-income countries in the Majority Worldfoot_0 , where poverty-related factors create barriers for early childhood development.

text.text: In South Africa, poverty hinders the quality of parent-child interactions that scaffold development by limiting learning resources in the home (e.g., lack of reading material).

Roughly 68% of children in South Africa live in poverty (Hall, 2025) and 46% of children under age five are already behind on developmental milestones (e.g., social-emotional learning [SEL], language, cognitive, and early literacy and numeracy skills; Tredoux et al., 2024).

text.text: Positive home learning environments and activities such as shared book reading promote early childhood development, particularly for children in higher-risk low-resource contexts.
However, implementing positive parenting practices can be challenging for parents precisely from such contexts.
Educational technologies (EdTech) have been promoted as a useful tool to support parents with reading resources and activities that advance child development.
Indeed, research on the positive use of EdTech such as digital books for young children in diverse contexts has begun to accumulate (see Kucirkova, 2018, for an overview).
text.formatted: Indeed, research on the positive use of EdTech such as digital books for young children in diverse contexts has begun to accumulate (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Kucirkova, 2018</ref>, for an overview).

text.text: However, this evidence base remains limited and rigorously designed impact evaluations of EdTech (i.e., randomized control trials; RCTs) are scant (Silverman et al., 2025).
text.formatted: However, this evidence base remains limited and rigorously designed impact evaluations of EdTech (i.e., randomized control trials; RCTs) are scant <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Silverman et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Recent work has called for the need to evaluate EdTech intervention studies on multiple indicators of quality, including their methodological quality, generalizability, and transparency (Kucirkova et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Recent work has called for the need to evaluate EdTech intervention studies on multiple indicators of quality, including their methodological quality, generalizability, and transparency <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Kucirkova et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Where evidence does exist, it is often limited to high-income countries in the Minority World instead of low-resource contexts with a disproportionate burden of low child development outcomes.
Beyond these challenges, when positive impacts of EdTech have been demonstrated in context, user engagement remains an issue.

For example, user retention rates are only about 2% after one month (Curry, 2026), highlighting the need to develop and test strategies that keep parents engaged with tools that have demonstrated positive impact.
text.formatted: For example, user retention rates are only about 2% after one month <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Curry, 2026)</ref>, highlighting the need to develop and test strategies that keep parents engaged with tools that have demonstrated positive impact.

text.text: This study provides an evaluation of a shared book reading and parenting EdTech App (BookSmart and Vroom Tips TM , henceforth abbreviated to BS-VT), and digital engagement strategies for caregivers and their children in South Africa, focusing on impacts on parenting practices and early childhood development.

Parenting practices that provide consistent stimulation within a supportive home environment play a central role in shaping children's cognitive, behavioral, and language development (Chang et al., 2009; National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine [NASEM], 2016).
text.formatted: Parenting practices that provide consistent stimulation within a supportive home environment play a central role in shaping children's cognitive, behavioral, and language development <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Chang et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr">National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine [NASEM], 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Practices such as shared reading, responsive communication, and developmentally appropriate scaffolding are especially influential because they provide learning opportunities and promote high-quality parent-child interactions.

Through experience, observation, feedback, and formal or informal information sources, parents form a system of knowledge, beliefs, and self-efficacy that shapes their parenting behavior and children's outcomes (Benedetto & Ingrassia, 2018; NASEM, 2016).
text.formatted: Through experience, observation, feedback, and formal or informal information sources, parents form a system of knowledge, beliefs, and self-efficacy that shapes their parenting behavior and children's outcomes <ref type="bibr">(Benedetto & Ingrassia, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">NASEM, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Parents' knowledge of child development, including age-appropriate expectations, strategies, and understanding of child social-emotional and cognitive needs, shapes how these practices are enacted and determines the quality of the home learning environment (NASEM, 2016; September et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Parents' knowledge of child development, including age-appropriate expectations, strategies, and understanding of child social-emotional and cognitive needs, shapes how these practices are enacted and determines the quality of the home learning environment <ref type="bibr">(NASEM, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">September et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Parental knowledge alone does not ensure effective practice, positive beliefs about parenting and parental self-efficacy (PSE) can increase the likelihood that those practices are translated into consistent, evidence-based parenting (NASEM, 2016).
text.formatted: Parental knowledge alone does not ensure effective practice, positive beliefs about parenting and parental self-efficacy (PSE) can increase the likelihood that those practices are translated into consistent, evidence-based parenting <ref type="bibr">(NASEM, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: PSE stems from accurate developmental knowledge, successful parenting experiences, and beliefs about the value of early investment, which strengthen confidence and persistence in effective parenting practices (Benedetto & Ingrassia, 2018; September et al., 2016).
text.formatted: PSE stems from accurate developmental knowledge, successful parenting experiences, and beliefs about the value of early investment, which strengthen confidence and persistence in effective parenting practices <ref type="bibr">(Benedetto & Ingrassia, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">September et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Parenting practices are highly influenced by socioeconomic status (SES).
Low-SES families with limited resources engage in positive parent-child interactions (e.g., activities that promote development) less frequently (Lurie et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Low-SES families with limited resources engage in positive parent-child interactions (e.g., activities that promote development) less frequently <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Lurie et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Lower-SES caregivers also tend to have less knowledge about developmental milestones and how parenting practices positively influence development (Bornstein et al., 2010) and thus, are less likely to believe that early childhood investments influence development (List et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Lower-SES caregivers also tend to have less knowledge about developmental milestones and how parenting practices positively influence development <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bornstein et al., 2010)</ref> and thus, are less likely to believe that early childhood investments influence development <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(List et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: EdTech interventions have the potential to address these disparities by providing low-cost, scalable, and accessible guidance that increases caregivers' knowledge, confidence, and opportunities to engage in developmentally supportive interactions with their children, particularly among families with limited access to traditional parenting resources.

EdTech interventions can improve parent-child interactions, literacy engagement, parenting knowledge, and PSE, although effects across studies are mixed and not consistently sustained over time (Jäggi et al., 2025; Kucirkova et al., 2025; Lin-Lewry et al., 2024).
text.formatted: EdTech interventions can improve parent-child interactions, literacy engagement, parenting knowledge, and PSE, although effects across studies are mixed and not consistently sustained over time <ref type="bibr">(Jäggi et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Kucirkova et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lin-Lewry et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: EdTech interventions related to observable parenting behaviors have been associated with greater caregiver involvement in shared reading and other literacy activities, stronger parent-child interactions, and more frequent use of developmentally supportive parenting practices, such as praise, responsive caregiving, and joint media engagement (Korin, 2021; Jäggi et al., 2025; Richert et al., 2025).
text.formatted: EdTech interventions related to observable parenting behaviors have been associated with greater caregiver involvement in shared reading and other literacy activities, stronger parent-child interactions, and more frequent use of developmentally supportive parenting practices, such as praise, responsive caregiving, and joint media engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Korin, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Jäggi et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Richert et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: For example, Jäggi et al. (2025) reviewed 13 digital parenting interventions and found generally positive effects on literacy engagement and parent-child communication.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr">Jäggi et al. (2025)</ref> reviewed 13 digital parenting interventions and found generally positive effects on literacy engagement and parent-child communication.

text.text: However, because the review included mixed study designs, the findings do not consistently support causal conclusions.
Evidence for improvements in PSE is less consistent.

In a meta-analysis of seven RCTs involving 1,342 new parents, which evaluated programs delivered through websites and mobile apps focusing on child development, and transition to parenthood, Lin-Lewry et al. (2024) found that EdTech interventions produced significant short-term improvements in PSE, perceived social support, and depressive symptoms.
text.formatted: In a meta-analysis of seven RCTs involving 1,342 new parents, which evaluated programs delivered through websites and mobile apps focusing on child development, and transition to parenthood, <ref type="bibr">Lin-Lewry et al. (2024)</ref> found that EdTech interventions produced significant short-term improvements in PSE, perceived social support, and depressive symptoms.

text.text: Thus, EdTech interventions may strengthen PSE by giving caregivers opportunities to learn, practice skills, and receive social support (Lin-Lewry et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Thus, EdTech interventions may strengthen PSE by giving caregivers opportunities to learn, practice skills, and receive social support <ref type="bibr">(Lin-Lewry et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, effect sizes varied across programs, and some trials found limited or no benefits, particularity for shorter interventions.
Overall, factors such as program duration, delivery modality, and the level of user engagement appear to shape both the size and sustainability of parenting outcomes.
Specific types of EdTech can also support children's SEL, cognition, language, and early literacy and numeracy skills.
For example, children can learn new vocabulary from developmentally appropriate digital media; e-books with interactive features reinforce rather than distract from the story (Richert et al., 2025).
text.formatted: For example, children can learn new vocabulary from developmentally appropriate digital media; e-books with interactive features reinforce rather than distract from the story <ref type="bibr">(Richert et al., 2025</ref>).

text.text: Shared parent-child reading of digital books has also been linked to improvements in language and reading (Bus et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Shared parent-child reading of digital books has also been linked to improvements in language and reading <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Bus et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Some apps also show promise for supporting social-emotional development (Hikmah et al., 2024); EdTech-based interventions have improved attention, impulse control, and adaptability among preschool-aged children (Yao & Abdullah, 2026).
text.formatted: Some apps also show promise for supporting social-emotional development <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hikmah et al., 2024)</ref>; EdTech-based interventions have improved attention, impulse control, and adaptability among preschool-aged children <ref type="bibr">(Yao & Abdullah, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In an RCT involving 74 preschoolers, Naumann et al. (2023) found that a six-week digital intervention program improved emotional regulation and reduced behavioral problems compared with a control condition. Hikmah et al. (2024) similarly found greater gains in SEL in children using interactive media than in children using traditional storybooks.

(2023)</ref> found that a six-week digital intervention program improved emotional regulation and reduced behavioral problems compared with a control condition. <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Hikmah et al. (2024)</ref> similarly found greater gains in SEL in children using interactive media than in children using traditional storybooks.

text.text: More broadly, apps and games built around prosocial content may strengthen empathy, cooperation, conflict resolution, and other social skills while reducing problematic behaviors (Richert et al., 2025; Naumann et al., 2023; Hikmah et al., 2024).
text.formatted: More broadly, apps and games built around prosocial content may strengthen empathy, cooperation, conflict resolution, and other social skills while reducing problematic behaviors <ref type="bibr">(Richert et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Naumann et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Hikmah et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Although developmentally-appropriate, research-informed EdTech has demonstrated meaningful benefits for children's learning and development, most commercially available digital products have little evidence of educational effectiveness (Korin, 2021; Richert et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Although developmentally-appropriate, research-informed EdTech has demonstrated meaningful benefits for children's learning and development, most commercially available digital products have little evidence of educational effectiveness <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Korin, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Richert et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: For example, an evaluation of the 124 most-downloaded educational apps found that most provided repetitive, distracting, and pedagogically weak experiences with limited learning value (Mayer et al., 2023).
text.formatted: For example, an evaluation of the 124 most-downloaded educational apps found that most provided repetitive, distracting, and pedagogically weak experiences with limited learning value <ref type="bibr">(Mayer et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, only one-quarter of the 100 most popular EdTech products used in U.S. schools had empirical evidence supporting their effectiveness (LearnPlatform, n.d.).
text.formatted: Similarly, only one-quarter of the 100 most popular EdTech products used in U.S. schools had empirical evidence supporting their effectiveness <ref type="bibr">(LearnPlatform, n.d.)</ref>.

text.text: Impact depends heavily on the quality of the technology, the evidence informing its design, the context in which it is used, caregiver involvement, and sustained user engagement (Richert et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Impact depends heavily on the quality of the technology, the evidence informing its design, the context in which it is used, caregiver involvement, and sustained user engagement <ref type="bibr">(Richert et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: A persistent challenge for EdTech parenting interventions is maintaining caregiver engagement over time.

Engagement with EdTech is typically highest immediately following enrollment and declines once its novelty has worn off, limiting opportunities for interventions to influence parenting behaviors and child development (Tsay et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Engagement with EdTech is typically highest immediately following enrollment and declines once its novelty has worn off, limiting opportunities for interventions to influence parenting behaviors and child development <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Tsay et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Many EdTech interventions incorporate behavioral science-based messaging strategies, or behavioral nudges, to encourage continued use.

These strategies are designed to reduce cognitive barriers (e.g., information overload, weariness), increase motivation, and prompt users to engage with the intervention, thereby increasing the likelihood that the intervention will achieve its intended effects (Balaskas et al., 2025).
text.formatted: These strategies are designed to reduce cognitive barriers (e.g., information overload, weariness), increase motivation, and prompt users to engage with the intervention, thereby increasing the likelihood that the intervention will achieve its intended effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Balaskas et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Nudges can be delivered through multiple channels (e.g., push notifications, text messages, emails) and may include simple reminders, or motivational or goal-setting prompts (Duckworth et al., 2025; Mayer et al., 2023; Kalil et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Nudges can be delivered through multiple channels (e.g., push notifications, text messages, emails) and may include simple reminders, or motivational or goal-setting prompts <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Duckworth et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Mayer et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kalil et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence suggests that the effectiveness of behavioral nudges depends on their content rather than simply their frequency.

Messages that target users' motivations or encourage goal setting have been shown to increase engagement more effectively than generic reminder nudges in some studies (Duckworth et al., 2025; Kalil et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Messages that target users' motivations or encourage goal setting have been shown to increase engagement more effectively than generic reminder nudges in some studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Duckworth et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kalil et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, some studies find that reminders alone can effectively increase engagement (Hansen & Andersen, 2025; York et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Conversely, some studies find that reminders alone can effectively increase engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Hansen & Andersen, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">York et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, greater engagement does not necessarily translate into impact.

For example, although goal-setting nudges increased app use, they did not improve children's literacy outcomes, possibly because caregivers engaged with the app to satisfy the prompts rather than to meaningfully participate in reading activities-a phenomenon described as the "nag factor" (Kalil et al., 2023).
text.formatted: For example, although goal-setting nudges increased app use, they did not improve children's literacy outcomes, possibly because caregivers engaged with the app to satisfy the prompts rather than to meaningfully participate in reading activities-a phenomenon described as the "nag factor" <ref type="bibr">(Kalil et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Behavioral nudges can be an important strategy for improving engagement, but their effectiveness depends on both the design of the messages and whether they promote meaningful participation rather than simply increasing app use.
To date, limited empirical work has compared different behavioral nudging strategies on parents' engagement with EdTech, and in turn, impacts on parenting practices and child outcomes.

The current study is a mixed-methods evaluation of BookSmart with built-in parenting tips (Vroom Tips TM ) and its impact on caregivers' self-efficacy, caregiving beliefs and practices, and early childhood outcomes (including SEL and problem behaviors, cognition, language, and early literacy and numeracy skills) in South Africa (Worldreader, n.d.; Vroom, n.d.).
text.formatted: The current study is a mixed-methods evaluation of BookSmart with built-in parenting tips (Vroom Tips TM ) and its impact on caregivers' self-efficacy, caregiving beliefs and practices, and early childhood outcomes (including SEL and problem behaviors, cognition, language, and early literacy and numeracy skills) in South Africa <ref type="bibr">(Worldreader, n.d.; Vroom, n.d.)</ref>.

text.text: The BookSmart application, developed by Worldreader, is a digital reading platform designed as a literacy-focused intervention that provides children-particularly those in low-resource settings-with access to reading materials.

BookSmart aims to achieve four primary goals: (1) to foster caregiver-child engagement in home reading, (2) to strengthen caregivers' self-efficacy in shared reading, (3) to promote children's early literacy development by emphasizing the pivotal role of caregivers in shaping early literacy experiences, and (4) to provide children with access to literary resources.
BookSmart also serves as a digital platform that includes access to Vroom's science-based parenting content (Vroom Tips TM ).
This enhanced version of the BookSmart platform embeds Vroom's practical "Brain Building" prompts within the reading experience.
Prompts were brief, play-based, and evidence-informed activities designed to help caregivers promote learning and development during everyday shared moments.
For example, "Snack Sorters" prompts children to group snacks together, encouraging them to learn shapes and colours (see Methods for more details).
Activities of this type support observational skills, language development, and interactive engagement.
The integration aims to simultaneously promote shared reading, strengthen caregiver-child relationships, and support early brain and literacy development.
Evidence from a previous evaluation in Kenya demonstrated that engagement with BookSmart effectively increased the frequency of parent-child reading interactions in the home.
Over 22 weeks, the frequency of reading with their child significantly increased and children's emergent literacy and vocabulary skills significantly improved (Kucirkova et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Over 22 weeks, the frequency of reading with their child significantly increased and children's emergent literacy and vocabulary skills significantly improved <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Kucirkova et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Total time spent reading was positively associated with improvements in children's pre-literacy skills.
Significant gains were also observed in children's social-emotional outcomes (Kucirkova et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Significant gains were also observed in children's social-emotional outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Kucirkova et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, maintaining caregiver engagement within the app remained a key challenge: caregiver-engagement with the app significantly decreased after 3 weeks of use, which could have diminished potential positive impacts (Kucirkova et al., 2025).
text.formatted: However, maintaining caregiver engagement within the app remained a key challenge: caregiver-engagement with the app significantly decreased after 3 weeks of use, which could have diminished potential positive impacts <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Kucirkova et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This study extends prior work by testing specific behavioral nudging strategies to increase caregiver engagement: reminder and goal-setting nudges.

Two studies were conducted: a 4-arm RCT to evaluate the impact of BS-VT with different behavioral nudging strategies, and a qualitative study to explore caregivers' experiences and challenges with the app.
Participants were randomized into four groups: BS-VT with goal-setting nudges, BS-VT with reminder nudges, BS-VT (no behavioral nudges), and a wait-listed control group.

We asked the following research questions: (1) Does BS-VT impact caregivers' self-efficacy, and caregiving beliefs and practices, and children's early childhood development (SEL and problem behaviors, cognitive, language, and early literacy and numeracy skills)?
(2) Do caregivers' use and engagement with BS-VT impact caregivers' self-efficacy, and caregiving beliefs and practices and impact children's early development?
(3) Do different behavioral nudging strategies (reminder nudges versus goal-setting nudges) impact caregivers' use and engagement with BS-VT?
Based on BookSmart's previous evaluation in Kenya, we predicted that caregiver's beliefs will positively shift following the use of BS-VT (Kucirkova et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Based on BookSmart's previous evaluation in Kenya, we predicted that caregiver's beliefs will positively shift following the use of BS-VT <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Kucirkova et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Children's developmental scores and caregiver self-efficacy, beliefs, and practices were predicted to improve following increased use and engagement with BS-VT.
Additionally, we predicted that use and engagement with BS-VT will improve with the addition of behavioral nudges.
Based on our theory of change (Figure 1), behavioral nudges would boost app usage, increasing positive caregiving processes, thereby impacting child developmental outcomes.
text.formatted: Based on our theory of change (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>), behavioral nudges would boost app usage, increasing positive caregiving processes, thereby impacting child developmental outcomes.

text.text: Study 2: Caregiver Experiences Using BookSmart and Vroom Tips TM Interviews with 20 caregivers further explored the role of BS-VT in households and caregivers' experiences with the app.

We asked: (1) in the context of everyday family life, how do caregivers describe their experience with the usability of BS-VT, (2) what challenges do caregivers face incorporating BS-VT into their daily routines, and (3) what suggestions do caregivers have for improving BS-VT use in real-life family settings?
This study aimed to address important gaps in the EdTech literature by providing a rigorous mixed-methods evaluation of an evidence-informed digital book reading and parenting intervention.

By combining experimental estimates of impact with qualitative insights into caregiver experiences, we examined whether BS-VT improves caregiver and child outcomes and how engagement influences its effectiveness.

In doing so, we contribute to the limited evidence base on EdTech in low-resource settings, informing the design and implementation of scalable digital interventions for young children and their families.
Caregivers who had at least one child between 3-5 years old residing in South Africa were recruited into the study in January 2026.

Prospective participants received a study invitation link randomized to one of four conditions: access to BS-VT and prompted with reminder nudges, access to the BS-VT and prompted with goal-setting nudges, access to the BS-VT app alone, or given no access to the BS-VT app.

These groups are henceforth referred to as the treatment groups (Reminder Nudges, Goal-Setting Nudges, BookSmart Alone, respectively), and the control group. 812 participants enrolled in the study and completed a baseline survey, see Figure 2.

Despite our best attempts to block their access to the app, some participants in the control group (n = 48) still signed onto BookSmart throughout the intervention (n = 30 engaged with BookSmart content).
Families were excluded from the study if they did not have a child between ages 3 to 5.

Children with developmental disabilities, including autism spectrum disorder, down syndrome, fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, fragile X syndrome, cerebral palsy, and ADHD, were included in the study.

Higher scores indicate stronger beliefs that caregiver engagement influences child outcomes.
Under 5 assessed caregiving practices, including cognitive stimulation and caregiver engagement in the home.
Caregivers were asked six questions about whether or not they or any other adult engaged in various activities (e.g., reading) with the child over the previous 3 days.
Responses were scored as either 2 for yes or 1 for no, and then summed.
assessed caregiver-child interactions and classified households as resilient, at risk, or neutral.

Caregivers rated interaction scenarios (e.g., I help my child learn by talking and showing him or her new things) using frequency response scales (e.g., "not very often," "sometimes," "often,"; "not very true," "not very true," "sometimes true," "mostly true.").

The Parents' Evaluation of Developmental Status: Developmental Milestones (PEDS:DM) assessed children's social-emotional, expressive and receptive language, and early literacy and numeracy (academic) skills.

For social-emotional and language skills, all tasks were administered and scored according to the PEDS:DM protocols, yielding separate scores for social-emotional skills, expressive language, and receptive language.

For academic skills, question 1 ("If you showed your child a penny and asked, 'What's this?', would he or she say penny or cent?") was omitted due to relevance concerns, as such, all children began with item 2.
social, problem solving (cognitive), and communication skills.
Caregivers were presented with scenarios of things their child may be able to do, or were prompted to ask their child a question and see how they responded.
Caregivers indicated whether their child could do each scenario with "yes" (10 points), "no" (0 points), or "sometimes" (5 points).
Points were summed for a final score in each domain, with higher scores indicating stronger skills.
Domain scores were then standardized according to the child's age group so scores could be compared across ages.
The Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) assessed children's social-emotional well-being and difficulties using age-appropriate caregiver-report items.
Caregivers rated each item as "not true," "somewhat true," or "certainly true."
Items were scored on a three-point scale, with positively worded items reverse-scored where required.
Scores were calculated for emotional symptoms, conduct problems, hyperactivity, peer problems, and prosocial behavior.
Internalizing difficulties were calculated as sum of emotional and peer-problem scores, and externalizing difficulties as sum of conduct and hyperactivity scores.
Higher prosocial scores indicated prosocial behavior; higher scores on all other domains indicated greater difficulties.

text.text: We also conducted Pearson's correlations of caregiver-and child-level outcomes and BS-VT engagement.

To address our first research question (intent-to-treat; ITT), we used multiple regression models with planned contrasts to examine whether treatment group predicted endline caregiver-and child-level outcomes, with baseline score, child age, and SES included as covariates.

Condition contrast vector was specified to contrast (1) no treatment (control group) versus treatment groups, (2) no behavioral nudges (BookSmart Alone group) versus behavioral nudges (Reminder and Goal-Setting Nudges groups), and (3) Reminder Nudges versus Goal-Setting Nudges.

To address our second research question (treatment-on-the-treated; ToT), we used multiple regression models to examine whether engagement with BS-VT (i.e., completing books or Vroom Tips TM ) predicted endline caregiver-and child-level outcomes, with baseline score, child age, and SES included as covariates.
Separate models were conducted using a binomial variable indicating whether the caregiver had any or no engagement, number of completed books, and number of completed Vroom Tips TM.
To address our third research question, we examined whether behavioral nudges (i.e., Goal-Setting Nudges, Reminder Nudges, no nudges) predicted engagement.
Separate models were conducted using a binomial variable indicating whether the caregiver had any or no engagement, number of completed books, and number of completed Vroom Tips TM as outcomes.
Where applicable, zero-inflated Poisson regression models were used to account for the high proportion of zero scores (n BookZeros = 267 [71%], n VroomTipsZeros = 309 [83%]).
All analyses were conducted using R (v4.5.1; R Core Team, 2025).
Caregiver outcomes were self-efficacy, beliefs about caregiver-child interactions, and caregiving practices.
Child outcomes were SEL and problem behaviors, cognition, language, and early literacy and numeracy (academic) skills.
Supplementary Materials provide additional details on constructs.

Separate models testing interactions between treatment group (question 1), or engagement (question 2) and age, SES, and baseline score, respectively, were conducted to examine treatment variation and are reported in Supplementary Materials.

To account for multiple comparisons, q values were generated within prespecified families of related hypotheses grouped by research question using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction (Benjamin & Hochberg, 1995); see Supplementary Materials for details.

We recruited 20 caregivers through MoyaApp, as in study 1, and followed the same inclusion and exclusion criteria with the following addition: families were excluded from the study if the caregiver was not female and between the ages 18 to 45.
A sample of 20 was selected with the intention of the study being exploratory.

Most in-depth interview studies achieve saturation with samples of 9-17 (Hennink & Kaiser, 2022), suggesting that our sample size should have provided sufficient results. 7 participants were caregivers of 3 year olds, 5 were caregivers of 4 year olds, and 8 were caregivers of 5 year olds.

text.text: The baseline interviews established what caregivers were already doing in their daily lives to help their child learn, and how capable they felt doing so.
In other words, the baseline interviews surfaced caregivers' starting point: their habits, mindsets, and gaps before exposure to BS-VT.
We asked caregivers about their daily interactions and shared reading routines and whether/how they integrated digital tools into these routines.

We also asked caregivers about their feelings of confidence and/or support needs for helping their child learn new things, and their beliefs about the importance of these everyday interactions for helping their child learn.
The endline interviews were both evaluative (did BS-VT add value?) and generative (what lessons and incentive structures can inform future iterations?).
We asked caregivers how they and their child used and felt about BS-VT, and the extent to which the tools fit into their daily routine.
We also asked the caregivers about their feelings towards the nudges, to understand whether the messages helped promote app usage.

Finally, we asked caregivers about their feelings of confidence and/or support needs for helping their child learn new things, their beliefs about the importance of these everyday interactions for helping their child learn, and how using BS-VT impacted their feelings of confidence, needs, and beliefs.
See Supplementary Materials for the complete baseline and endline interview questions.

BS-VT usage metrics were tracked for each participant, including the number of times the app was used, the total time (seconds) spent in the app, the number of books completed, and the number of Vroom Tips TM completed.
Participants completed a baseline interview between November 3 and November 14, 2025.
Afterwards, they were prompted to use BS-VT for an intervention period of 3 weeks.

The interviews were coded by four members of the research team using Dedoose software (Dedoose Version 10.0.59, 2025) and following a combination deductive-inductive thematic analysis approach (Braun & Clarke, 2006).

text.text: The interview questions were based on the mechanisms by which EdTech and caregiving practices relate to child learning and development outcomes, as illuminated by existing academic literature (e.g., self-efficacy, beliefs, knowledge, shared reading, caregiving practices, app engagement, accessibility).
An initial set of a priori codes was generated based on the content of the interviews and the aforementioned mechanisms of interest.
The a priori codes were grouped according to a priori themes developed based on our research questions.
See Supplementary Materials for details.
Usage varied widely.
App usage declined slightly over the course of the intervention period, however, the average number of books completed increased.
Some participants used the app very little, while others spent significant amounts of time in the app and completed several books and Vroom Tips TM .
Importantly, Vroom Tips TM usage was quite low overall.
The vast majority of participants did not open or complete any Vroom Tips TM .

text.text: Motivation is Academic ('School Readiness').
The interviews suggested that caregivers were highly motivated to read with their child.

Caregivers saw a direct link between reading and speech and vocabulary skill development, and their motivation was driven by a desire for children to master the English language and succeed in Grade R (i.e., compulsory year of education prior to Grade 1).
Participant Q040 reflected, "My five-year-old didn't speak or utter many words… So I started reading.
Then yes, his tongue became easier to say [words]."
text.formatted: Then yes, his tongue became easier to say <ref type="bibr">[words]</ref>."

text.text: Overall, it seemed that caregivers viewed shared reading as more of an educational duty instead of a recreational or bonding activity.
The Confidence-Support Paradox.
The interviews illuminated an interesting contradiction related to caregiver confidence and self-efficacy.
Caregivers felt confident in their ability to support their child's learning and development.
However, they explicitly requested support in the form of guidance or reminders.

Participant Q049 said, "Yes, I do feel confident… [my child] react[s] when I'm playing with them, when I'm teaching them", but also explained that being too busy limits their everyday interactions with their child, and expressed a desire for resources on how to better support their child's learning.
In other words, their confidence was high, but they also needed support.
These findings suggest that although caregivers feel capable of supporting their child's learning, the logistics of everyday life overwhelm their capabilities.
The Resource Gap and 'Latent Demand'.
Not only did they feel overwhelmed, but caregivers also noted significant gaps in physical reading and learning resources.
Most of the caregivers reported that their households owned fewer than three children's books; they often relied on books and materials sent home from school.
They also mentioned the cost of books and fatigue from working late shifts as barriers to shared reading.
Caregivers expressed that they wanted to read more frequently, even daily, if it were not for these barriers.
Participant Q034 told us, "If I had more books and more time, I would read every day.
But right now, we just have the school books."

These barriers may have contributed to caregivers' perception of shared reading being purely a means to a developmental end; they did not have the time, energy, or resources for shared reading to be a fun, recreational activity.
Moreover, although smartphones were ubiquitous among the caregivers we interviewed, they were not viewed as reading and learning resources.
Prior to the BS-VT intervention, caregivers and their children primarily used devices for passive entertainment, such as watching cartoons on YouTube.
Due to the high cost of cellular data in South Africa, caregivers expressed hesitance about depleting their airtime by clicking unknown links or exploring new educational apps.
Data cost is therefore a major barrier for caregivers who might otherwise seek out digital resources to supplement the few physical books and learning resources they have in their home.
Thus, the data-free nature of the MoyaApp environment is a crucial prerequisite for engagement with apps like BookSmart, making them accessible regardless of cost barriers.

Since households had limited reading and educational materials and toys, caregivers relied heavily on everyday household activities and routines to provide incidental learning opportunities for their child.
Caregivers told us they count vegetables while cooking, name colors while doing laundry, and sing songs while completing chores with their child.
They also cited unstructured outdoor play as the primary method of promoting their child's physical and social development.
The 'Digital Unlock': Access Trumps Preference.
Although some caregivers reported feeling a sentimental preference for physical books, they were driven to use BookSmart by the convenience it offered.

Participant Q078 expressed a preference for physical books, but also showed appreciation for BookSmart by saying, "they have a lot of books… there's a variety of choice… [and] we don't have access to a library".
text.formatted: Participant Q078 expressed a preference for physical books, but also showed appreciation for BookSmart by saying, "they have a lot of books… there's a variety of choice… <ref type="bibr">[and]</ref> we don't have access to a library".

text.text: With BookSmart, caregivers were able to "carry a library" in their pocket, allowing them to read with their child during idle moments when they previously would not have.
The participants also appreciated the sheer volume of diverse children's stories available, feeling that BookSmart addressed the reading resource scarcity they felt prior to the intervention period.
The intervention seemed to shift caregivers' perceptions of the smartphone as a passive entertainment device to an educational tool.
Caregivers relayed that the app did not replace physical interactions and books.

Some caregivers mentioned that their children wanted to turn pages or touch the phone while reading, or take the phone outside like they would with physical books; things they are unable to do with their caregivers' smartphone.
A few caregivers also discussed the challenge of "shared focus" on a small screen, with notifications and incoming calls sometimes disrupting the reading flow.

It seems that BookSmart did not replace physical books, but it did supplement the reading resources they were lacking and provided benefits that physical books could not, like the ability to read anywhere and anytime.
Overall, caregivers appreciated the reminders to use BS-VT.
They saw the reminders as helpful prompts that supported their ability to create a habit out of using BS-VT with their child.
However, a minority of participants did not see the messages, which may have limited their app usage.
As participant Q054 explained, "I didn't see the messages… if I had the reminder, I would have remembered to read more."
This may have been due to individual user's MoyaApp notification settings.
The Language Barrier and the 'Translation Burden'.
Despite the overall positive experience that caregivers had with BookSmart, a major friction point was the dominance of English reading content.
South Africa is a multilingual country, and many children are native speakers of a non-English language (e.g., isiZulu, isiXhosa, Venda, etc.) which may be the primary language spoken in the home.
Caregivers reported reading the English text silently and then narrating the story in their home language to help their child understand.
Participant Q040 explained, "I read in English and translate into [home language]... it helps them understand, but having books in our language would be better."

Caregivers expressed the desire for their children to learn English, the lack of stories in home languages forced caregivers to act as real-time translators, requiring a high cognitive load while reading with their child.
There is a clear, unmet demand for content in home languages to make the reading experience more culturally resonant.

We examined how caregivers in South Africa engaged with a digital reading and parenting platform, BookSmart with embedded parenting tips-Vroom Tips™ (BS-VT), as a resource for supporting young children's learning through shared book reading and everyday caregiver-child interactions.

Across two mixed-methods studies, we focused on how this EdTech parenting intervention impacted caregiver self-efficacy, beliefs, and practices, and children's early developmental outcomes, as well as factors that supported or constrained engagement.
EdTech parenting interventions are often proposed as a scalable means of expanding developmental opportunities for children in low-resource contexts.
Our findings suggest that this promise depends on an important distinction between access to developmental resources and engagement in developmentally-supportive experiences.

Providing caregivers with access to BS-VT produced limited impacts on caregiver and child outcomes, however, nudging caregivers to engage with BS-VT produced positive child outcomes, including stronger academic (early literacy and numeracy), cognitive, and language skills, specifically for more vulnerable children (i.e., children from lower-SES families and children with lower baseline skills)-albeit these effects were mostly marginally significant (p < .05 and q < .1) and did not meet our threshold for statistical significance (q < .05).
text.formatted: Providing caregivers with access to BS-VT produced limited impacts on caregiver and child outcomes, however, nudging caregivers to engage with BS-VT produced positive child outcomes, including stronger academic (early literacy and numeracy), cognitive, and language skills, specifically for more vulnerable children (i.e., children from lower-SES families and children with lower baseline skills)-albeit these effects were mostly marginally significant (p < .05 and q < .1) and did not meet our threshold for statistical significance (q < .05).

text.text: Viewed alongside caregivers' accounts of the practical and contextual barriers that shaped BS-VT engagement, these findings suggest that the potential of EdTech parenting interventions to influence child development depends on whether families can integrate parenting content into sustained, meaningful caregiver-child interactions.

This distinction is particularly relevant in contexts where socioeconomic disadvantage can constrain developmental opportunities and families face greater barriers to consistently enacting developmentally-supportive practices.
Simply having access to EdTech resources did not produce positive outcomes in caregiving practices or child outcomes.
However, caregiver engagement with BS-VT was marginally linked to higher literacy and numeracy skills, and reading more books significantly predicted higher language skills.

These findings add to the growing body of research suggesting that EdTech tools can successfully support early child development (Hikmah et al., 2024; Kucirkova et al., 2025; Naumann et al., 2023; Richert et al., 2025), but they critically emphasize the need for sustained engagement.
text.formatted: These findings add to the growing body of research suggesting that EdTech tools can successfully support early child development <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hikmah et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Kucirkova et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Naumann et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Richert et al., 2025)</ref>, but they critically emphasize the need for sustained engagement.

text.text: A substantial body of research has established that shared reading, responsive communication, and cognitively stimulating activities support children's language, cognitive, and social-emotional development by providing opportunities for learning within everyday caregiver-child interactions (e.g., NASEM, 2016).

EdTech parenting interventions may help facilitate these processes by providing caregivers with accessible reading materials, developmentally appropriate activities, and practical guidance for incorporating learning opportunities into daily routines.

Interestingly, while completing parenting tips was positively associated with child outcomes, we found that when caregivers with a higher baseline self-efficacy completed more parenting tips, they were more likely to report lower self-efficacy at endline.
Before using BS-VT, interviews with caregivers revealed they felt confident in their caregiving abilities, but desired more support in the form of resources and time.

It's possible that after using Vroom Tips TM -which are activities designed to help promote development during brief everyday shared moments-caregivers became exposed to new information about parenting practices, which may have altered caregivers understanding of effective parenting and the standards against which they evaluate their own practice, leading to an adjustment in their self-efficacy.

Caregiver-child interactions are shaped by a complex interplay of caregivers' developmental knowledge, self-efficacy, opportunities to engage in supporting parenting practices, and beliefs about the importance of such practices.
Parenting interventions often aim to strengthen these constructs simultaneously, however, changes in knowledge and practices may not immediately correspond to improvements in parenting efficacy.

This highlights the need for a more nuanced understanding of how digital parenting interventions influence the interrelated processes of acquiring developmental knowledge, adopting new parenting practices, and evaluating one's own parenting competence.
Future research should examine how these processes unfold over time.
A persistent challenge for digital parenting interventions is translating initial access into sustained engagement.

Previous research has documented substantial declines in engagement with EdTech interventions over time, potentially limiting their ability to produce sustained changes in parenting practices and child development (Kucirkova et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Previous research has documented substantial declines in engagement with EdTech interventions over time, potentially limiting their ability to produce sustained changes in parenting practices and child development <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Kucirkova et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This challenge may be particularly consequential for parenting interventions, where developmental benefits are expected to accumulate through repeated opportunities for responsive interaction and cognitive stimulation rather than isolated exposure to intervention content.
Implementing behavioral nudging strategies that can produce sustained engagement into digital parenting tools is therefore key.
Engagement with BS-VT overall remained low in this study, with 52% of treated participants having accessed the app and only 39% of those who accessed it read a book or completed a parenting tip.
However, caregivers who received nudges completed more parenting tips (q <. 05) and read more books (q < .1) compared to caregivers who were not nudged.
text.formatted: However, caregivers who received nudges completed more parenting tips (q <. 05) and read more books (q < .1) compared to caregivers who were not nudged.

text.text: This adds to an emerging literature showing that nudge-based parenting interventions can change parental investments and child outcomes, including in the United States (York et al., 2019), Brazil (Bettinger et al., 2022), and Costa Rica (Angrist et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This adds to an emerging literature showing that nudge-based parenting interventions can change parental investments and child outcomes, including in the United States <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(York et al., 2019)</ref>, Brazil <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bettinger et al., 2022)</ref>, and Costa Rica <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Angrist et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, the format of the behavioral nudge mattered.
Caregivers who received goal-setting nudges completed more parenting tips than caregivers who received reminder nudges, suggesting that goal-setting may be more effective at promoting engagement.
This corroborates previous studies (Duckworth et al., 2025; Kalil et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This corroborates previous studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Duckworth et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kalil et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: For example, Kalil et al. (2023) found that reminder nudges were associated with a decrease in child skills.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr">Kalil et al. (2023)</ref> found that reminder nudges were associated with a decrease in child skills.

text.text: Unlike repeated reminders, which may feel intrusive or controlling to busy caregivers, the self-endorsed goals in goal-setting nudges may preserve autonomy by allowing caregivers to choose and initiate their own targets.

Consistent with self-determination theory (Ryan and Deci, 2000), this autonomy-supportive design may sustain motivation and improve engagement without undermining interaction quality (Kalil et al., 2023; Balaskas et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Consistent with self-determination theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Ryan and Deci, 2000)</ref>, this autonomy-supportive design may sustain motivation and improve engagement without undermining interaction quality <ref type="bibr">(Kalil et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Balaskas et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, caregiver interviews indicated that they appreciated the nudges they received, and felt they were useful.
Care was taken to create engaging messages that included animations, parenting modeling videos, and novel content that did not repeat across messages.
These strategies may offer a viable solution for promoting engagement with interventions that improve child outcomes.
Importantly, not only did goal-setting nudges increase caregiver engagement, but they made a meaningful impact on children's outcomes.

The "fade-in" hypothesis suggests that intervention impacts become detectable only after participants have integrated new practices into their daily routine (Mayer et al., 2023)-our findings suggest goal-setting nudges support this integration and may have been particularly useful for families navigating competing demands associated with socioeconomic disadvantage.
text.formatted: The "fade-in" hypothesis suggests that intervention impacts become detectable only after participants have integrated new practices into their daily routine <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Mayer et al., 2023)</ref>-our findings suggest goal-setting nudges support this integration and may have been particularly useful for families navigating competing demands associated with socioeconomic disadvantage.

text.text: Here, we found that children from lower SES households and children with low baseline scores showed positive impacts in social-emotional, cognitive, and language skills when caregivers received behavioral nudges, albeit these effects were largely marginally significant (q < .1).
