text.text: Similarly, a SMS-based parent nudging intervention in Côte d'Ivoire showed no overall impacts on child learning outcomes, yet subgroup analyses revealed that nudges produced larger improvements in learning specifically for children with low baseline learning levels (Wolf & Lichand, 2023).
text.formatted: Similarly, a SMS-based parent nudging intervention in Côte d'Ivoire showed no overall impacts on child learning outcomes, yet subgroup analyses revealed that nudges produced larger improvements in learning specifically for children with low baseline learning levels <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Wolf & Lichand, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Socioeconomic disadvantage is associated with disparities in access to learning materials and opportunities for cognitively stimulating caregiver-child interactions, contributing to inequalities in early developmental outcomes, even when caregivers recognize the importance of supporting their children's development (Lurie et al., 2021; NASEM, 2016).
text.formatted: Socioeconomic disadvantage is associated with disparities in access to learning materials and opportunities for cognitively stimulating caregiver-child interactions, contributing to inequalities in early developmental outcomes, even when caregivers recognize the importance of supporting their children's development <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Lurie et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">NASEM, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: By providing low-cost access to reading resources and developmentally appropriate parenting activities, EdTech interventions may help address some of the material constraints on the home learning environment, highlighting the potential of digital parenting interventions to reduce inequalities in children's developmental opportunities.
However, the same socioeconomic conditions that increase the potential value of EdTech interventions may also constrain families' ability to benefit from them.
Access to a platform does not necessarily imply equitable opportunities for meaningful engagement.

Differences in device availability and quality, connectivity, digital literacy, language accessibility, and competing household demands may influence whether caregivers can incorporate EdTech resources into everyday routines.
Indeed, our finding that SES predicted completion of parenting tips suggests that engagement with EdTech interventions is socio-economically driven.

Interviews with caregivers corroborate these challenges: caregivers noted their hesitation around depleting their airtime, highlighting the importance of offering cost-free access, particularly for low-SES families.
Language barriers also served as a challenge for caregivers-half reported that they translated stories for their children in real time.
BookSmart consists of English-dominant content, while South Africa is highly multilingual with 12 official languages and many additional languages spoken throughout the country.

Digital parenting interventions face an important equity challenge: while they may expand opportunities for disadvantaged children, unequal engagement could reproduce or exacerbate existing inequalities.

A central implication of our findings is that EdTech tools, such as BS-VT, can support parenting and early childhood development (Hikmah et al., 2024; Kucirkova et al., 2025; Naumann et al., 2023; Richert et al., 2025), but engagement with the intervention is critical to realizing positive outcomes.
text.formatted: A central implication of our findings is that EdTech tools, such as BS-VT, can support parenting and early childhood development <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hikmah et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Kucirkova et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Naumann et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Richert et al., 2025)</ref>, but engagement with the intervention is critical to realizing positive outcomes.

text.text: Targeting user engagement is a key determinant of an intervention's effectiveness; even well-designed, evidence-based EdTech applications are unlikely to improve caregiving or child development if users do not engage with them consistently.
Behavioral nudges, especially goal-setting prompts, may be particularly helpful for driving engagement (Duckworth et al., 2025; Kalil et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Behavioral nudges, especially goal-setting prompts, may be particularly helpful for driving engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Duckworth et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kalil et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, reducing costs for users to access digital tools can ensure that tools remain equitable and that families can benefit from the learning opportunities they provide, regardless of any socioeconomic barriers.

More broadly, these findings underscore the importance of rigorous, context-sensitive evaluations of digital parenting interventions, particularly in low-resource settings where evidence of effectiveness remains limited.

Randomized controlled trials provide an important means of establishing whether EdTech interventions produce measurable improvements in caregiver and child outcomes, while analyses of engagement and qualitative investigations can help identify the processes and contextual conditions that may shape effectiveness.
Several important limitations and directions for future research should be considered.
Our findings may have been limited by the length of the intervention.

The full potential effects of engagement with BS-VT on parenting and child outcomes may require more time to emerge; a longer intervention period may have allowed caregivers more time to integrate BS-VT into their daily routines (Mayer et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The full potential effects of engagement with BS-VT on parenting and child outcomes may require more time to emerge; a longer intervention period may have allowed caregivers more time to integrate BS-VT into their daily routines <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Mayer et al., 2023</ref>).

text.text: It's also important to note that several effects did not meet the threshold for statistical significance (q < .05), but were marginally significant (p < .05 and q < .1) and caution should be applied when interpreting these findings.
text.formatted: It's also important to note that several effects did not meet the threshold for statistical significance (q < .05), but were marginally significant (p < .05 and q < .1) and caution should be applied when interpreting these findings.

text.text: Additionally, engagement data was limited by indicators that captured whether caregivers completed books or parenting tips, but not the quality of engagement.
Caregivers may have completed books or parenting tips when children were tired or distracted, with limited conversation or responsive interaction.

Engagement may have also been impacted by technical challenges beyond the control of the research team: e.g., some participants in the nudges groups may have not received nudges due their notification settings, potentially limiting their engagement with BS-VT.

Future research should examine how digital parenting interventions become integrated into caregivers' everyday interactions with young children, including how behavioral nudges may shape the frequency and quality of these interactions, and which forms of engagement are most consequential for children's cognitive, language, and social-emotional development.

Larger longitudinal studies incorporating multiple measurement points would also help clarify how caregiver and child outcomes evolve as families adopt new parenting practices and identify contextual factors that facilitate or constrain these benefits, particularly in low-resource settings.

These studies (1) evaluated the impact of a digital reading intervention, BookSmart, and its embedded parenting tips, Vroom Tips TM (BS-VT), on caregiver and early childhood outcomes in South Africa and (2) explored the role of behavioral nudging strategies in supporting sustained engagement over time.
Our findings show that providing access to EdTech resources alone is insufficient to produce meaningful developmental benefits.

Rather, the potential of these interventions depends on caregivers' engagement with developmentally supportive content and opportunities to integrate this content into everyday caregiver-child interactions.

Behavioral nudges may help bridge the gap between access and engagement, with our findings suggesting particular potential for supporting children experiencing socioeconomic and developmental disadvantage.

By combining experimental estimates of intervention impact with measures of engagement and qualitative accounts of families' experiences, the present study provides insights into both the potential and limitations of digital parenting interventions.
Such evaluations are essential for informing the development of interventions that are not only scalable and accessible, but also capable of producing meaningful and equitable developmental benefits.

Study 1 -Participant Recruitment MoyaApp is a free-to-download super app in South Africa that features messaging, voice, and video calling capabilities, and houses content, resources, and services (see MoyaApp, n.d.).

Importantly, MoyaApp works even when a user has no airtime or data balance, ensuring that access to messaging, resources, and content (including BookSmart) is data free and therefore not cost prohibitive.
MoyaApp users can consent to being contacted for research participation during the signup process.

An initial screening process was conducted by MoyaApp to identify potential participants who fit the study's eligibility criteria using information provided to MoyaApp as part of the user signup and research contact consent process (i.e., age, caregiver status, BookSmart use, MoyaApp activity). 6000 survey links were generated and randomized to one of four groups: the control group, the BookSmart Alone, the BookSmart and Goal-Setting Messages group, or the BookSmart and Reminder Messages group. 3429 users detected through the initial screening process were sent a survey link through REDCap, a secure, web-based data collection platform (Harris et al., 2009; 2019).
text.formatted: An initial screening process was conducted by MoyaApp to identify potential participants who fit the study's eligibility criteria using information provided to MoyaApp as part of the user signup and research contact consent process (i.e., age, caregiver status, BookSmart use, MoyaApp activity). 6000 survey links were generated and randomized to one of four groups: the control group, the BookSmart Alone, the BookSmart and Goal-Setting Messages group, or the BookSmart and Reminder Messages group. 3429 users detected through the initial screening process were sent a survey link through REDCap, a secure, web-based data collection platform <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Harris et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2019)</ref>.

text.text: Recruitment began January 22, 2026 and was discontinued March 17, 2026 after reaching the target sample size (N = 634).

An oversample of 28% (N = 178) was recruited to act as a retention buffer group to account attrition throughout the study; however, attrition was greater than expected due to some technical issues with the app, leading to underpowered analyses.
After opening the baseline survey link, potential participants were required to pass two additional screening checkpoints to ensure we only captured responses from eligible participants.
They were first asked to select the age ranges of children they care for.
If they indicated they care for a child between 3 to 5 years old, they proceeded to the consent form detailing their participation in the study.
In this form, five comprehension questions were administered.
If more than two comprehension questions were completed incorrectly, participants were deemed ineligible for the study.
This was done for two primary reasons.
First, from an ethical standpoint, it was essential to ensure that all participants were fully informed about the study before providing consent.
Incorrect responses indicated that an individual may not have adequately understood the study procedures, risks, or expectations, thereby undermining the validity of their informed consent.
Second, adequate reading comprehension was a practical requirement for participation.
The study involved caregiver engagement in shared reading activities, a central component of both the intervention and the BookSmart program.

Participants who were unable to correctly answer comprehension questions might face challenges in understanding the materials or effectively participating in the reading activities, which could compromise both the fidelity of the intervention and the integrity of the study outcomes.

Those who passed the comprehension questions and consented to the study proceeded to the survey where they were first asked to provide birth dates for their child(ren) between 3 and 5 years old, to confirm that their children are in the target age range.
Ineligible participants did not complete the remainder of the survey, which administered all study measures.
Caregiver education attainment was scored on a scale of 0 to 10, ranging from no schooling to having received a doctorate.
Household monthly income was scored on a scale of 0 to 13, ranging from no income to more than R100 000.
For each item indicated in the household inventory, one point was assigned for up to 22 points possible.

The Macarthur Scale of Subjective Social Status asked caregivers to consider income, education, and employment, then place themself on a ladder depending on where they believed they stood in reference to other people in 1) South Africa, and 2) in their community.
The bottom of the ladder (i.e., 1) represented people in the lowest standing, while the top of the ladder (i.e., 10) represented the highest standing (e.g., most money, most education).
The Global Scales for Early Development (GSED) was used to assess generalized development of children up to 36 months of age across diverse cultures and contexts.
This assessment was only administered to children aged 3 and older children who scored below age level on the PEDS:DM assessment.
We used the short form, caregiver-reported edition of the GSED.
Scoring was completed following the instructions provided with the GSED.
Note that only 40% of the sample completed the GSED (n = 210) due to the narrower age range and therefore this measure is only reported in the Supplementary Materials.
An additional survey section was administered to the treatment groups at endline to further assess their use of BS-VT.

This section asked about: (1) how frequently participants used BookSmart with their child (e.g., every day, once per week, never), (2) how frequently they used Vroom Tips TM (e.g., every day, once per week, never), (3) how frequently they engaged with the in-app suggested activities (i.e., every time, some of the time, or never), and (4) any previous use of BookSmart (i.e., yes or no).
This section also asked participants questions about their satisfaction with BS-VT.

These questions assessed their (1) overall satisfaction with BS-VT (e.g., somewhat satisfied, accompanied by a written response), (2) reasons as to why they may have not used the app (e.g., not enough time, child does not enjoy it), (3) average comprehension of suggested activities (i.e., always, most of the time, some of the time, or never).

SEPTI: Most area's scores (i.e., caregiver language and reading difficulties, shared caregiver-child reading time, learning techniques used in the home, household access to children's books) were calculated as item means, whereas caregiver self-efficacy was calculated as an item sum.
Subjective Caregiver Beliefs: Three hypothetical scenarios were presented under both conditions (i.e., interactive and non-interactive caregiving).
Difference scores between the two conditions were calculated for each scenario and averaged to create a total caregiver involvement belief score.
Caregivers had to correctly answer screener questions (i.e., identifying where 25 and 75 were on a slider and which of 25 and 75 were larger) for scores to be included in the relevant analyses.

Caregiver outcomes were operationalized as the following constructs: (1) caregiver self-efficacy (SEPTI Caregiver Self-Efficacy), (2) caregiver's beliefs about caregiver-child interactions, and (3) caregiving practices (composite of SEPTI Shared Caregiver-Child Reading Time, SEPTI Learning Techniques Used in the Home, MICS cognitive stimulation and caregiver engagement in the home, and BPCIS household risk, resilience, or neutrality).

Child outcomes were operationalized as the following constructs: (1) SEL (composite of PEDS:DM social-emotional skills, SDQ prosocial skills, and ASQ-3 personal social skills measured) and problem behaviors (SDQ internalizing and externalizing difficulties), ( 2) cognition (ASQ-3 child problem solving skills), (3) language (composite of PEDS:DM receptive and expressive language skills, and ASQ-3 communication skills), and (4) early literacy and numeracy (academic) skills (PEDS:DM academic skills).
text.formatted: Child outcomes were operationalized as the following constructs: (1) SEL (composite of PEDS:DM social-emotional skills, SDQ prosocial skills, and ASQ-3 personal social skills measured) and problem behaviors (SDQ internalizing and externalizing difficulties), ( <ref type="formula">2</ref>) cognition (ASQ-3 child problem solving skills), (3) language (composite of PEDS:DM receptive and expressive language skills, and ASQ-3 communication skills), and (4) early literacy and numeracy (academic) skills (PEDS:DM academic skills).

text.text: A composite score (composed of the two Macarthur Scale of Subjective Social Status questions, household income, caregiver education, and household amenities) was calculated for household SES to act as a covariate.
Caregiver and child variables that went into composites were examined as individual outcomes in our secondary analyses.

We also examined two unique outcomes in our secondary analyses: generalized development of children (GSED development) and child development (composite of PEDS:DM receptive and expressive language, PEDS:DM social-emotional skills, ASQ-3 communication, problem solving, and personal social skills, SDQ prosocial skills, SDQ internalizing and externalizing difficulties, and GSED development).

Use and engagement with BS-VT was operationalized as the number of books completed in BookSmart, the number of Vroom Tips TM completed, and as a dichotomous engagement variable: if a participant completed any books or Vroom Tips TM throughout the intervention, they were scored as "yes" for having engaged, otherwise participants were scored as "no".
Notably, we removed outliers (n = 4, 1% of sample), defined as participants in the 99th percentile, for the number of completed books or Vroom Tips TM when examining our third research question.
This method was used as standard inter-quartile outlier methods did not suit the zero-inflated data and to minimize the number of data points eliminated.
Composite scores were created following the method of Anderson (2008).
text.formatted: Composite scores were created following the method of <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Anderson (2008)</ref>.

text.text: Each component score is first standardized, then the composite is created from the weighted average of each component score.
Weights are determined by the inverse of the covariance matrix of the standardized scores.
Notably, for any participants who had missing scores for any given variable (i.e., they chose not to respond), their score was calculated using a covariance matrix that excluded this variable.
If a participant only had one scored variable in the composite, they were excluded from the relevant analyses.

Due to technical issues, some participants' child's age was calculated as 0 when completing their endline survey, causing them to not see most of the child measures (all but the PEDS:DM academic skill questions were hidden).
As such, children with an endline age of 0 were excluded (n = 30, 6% of sample) from models examining child outcomes.
To account for multiple comparisons, we generated q values.

Each research question had its own calculation for q values, creating three sets for main models (RQ1, RQ2, RQ3), and four sets for supplementary models (RQ1: secondary outcome main models; RQ1: all interaction models; RQ2: secondary outcome main models; RQ2: all interaction models).

An initial screening process was conducted by MoyaApp to identify potential participants, as in study 1.100 users matching this criteria were sent a survey link through REDCap in which they needed to pass two additional screening checkpoints.
Potential participants were first asked to select the age ranges of the children they care for.

If they indicated that they have a child within the age range of 3-5 years old, they proceeded to the next form where they were informed about the study requirements and were asked whether they consent to participate.

Those who consented proceeded to the pilot survey where they were first asked to provide birth dates for their child(ren) between 3 and 5 years old, to confirm that their children are in the target age range.
Ineligible participants did not complete the remainder of the survey.
After receiving survey responses, the research team messaged participants via WhatsApp to schedule the semi-structured interviews.
Participants completed a baseline interview between November 3 and November 14, 2025.
Afterwards, they were prompted to use BS-VT for an intervention period of 3 weeks.
During this time, they received 3 messages through MoyaApp's messaging system reminding them to use BS-VT.
The interviewer also sent instructions to participants on how to access BookSmart.
BS-VT usage and engagement were monitored during the 3-week intervention period.
Participants were then messaged via WhatsApp to participate in the endline interview, which took place between November 25 and December 5, 2025.
All interviews were conducted remotely through WhatsApp audio calls to ensure accessibility and low data usage.
Interviews were recorded using Loom (Loom, n.d.) and transcribed using Fireflies.ai (Fireflies.ai, n.d.).
text.formatted: Interviews were recorded using Loom (Loom, n.d.) and transcribed using Fireflies.ai <ref type="bibr">(Fireflies.ai, n.d.)</ref>.

Study 2 -Data Analysis Baseline coding themes of interest included: caregiver-child learning activities, reading practices, reading aspirations, caregiver confidence, resources and barriers, technology use, perceived importance of reading, and child agency.

Endline coding themes of interest included: BookSmart usage, BookSmart app perception, Vroom Tips TM usage, Vroom Tips TM perception, overall suggestions/confidence change/continue use, language, reminder, and motivation.
Although we began coding with the a priori codes, in line with a combination deductive-inductive approach, we added additional codes as needed.
These additional codes were developed inductively based on patterns that emerged from the interview data.
Subsequently, codes and themes were refined throughout the analysis process.
Tables S1 and S2 outline the final codes and themes.

Of the participants in the three treatment conditions, 8 (BookSmart Alone n = 2, Goal-Setting Messages n = 4, Reminder Messages n = 2) accessed BookSmart throughout the intervention.
Additionally, of the participants who accessed BookSmart, only 2 (25%) completed a book or Vroom Tip TM within it.
The small sample size (n = 19) limits any inferential statistical analyses.

However, a two-sample proportion test was conducted to determine if there was a statistically significant difference in the proportion of participants who accessed between caregivers of children with disabilities (n₁ = 8, p̂₁ = .42) and caregivers of neurotypical children (n₂ = 312, p̂₂ = .52).
The results were not statistically significant (2 = 0.389, p = 0.532) indicating that usage is similar between the two sub-samples.

Notably, despite our best attempts to block their access to the app, some participants in the control group (n = 48) still signed onto BookSmart throughout the intervention.
The most popular Vroom Tip TM type was tips for during snacktime, with 111 of these tips completed by participants through the intervention.

Their popularity was followed by tips targeting early learning moments during playtime (n = 54), tips targeted towards expecting caregivers or those with very young children (i.e., less than 2 years old; n = 30), tips for when families were cleaning up (n = 23), and tips for when families were on the go (n = 23).

Other tips completed included tips for when families were doing laundry (n = 20), tips for during mealtime (n = 19), tips for when families were getting dressed (n = 15), tips for during bedtime (n = 14), tips for during bathtime (n = 11), tips for "anytime, anywhere" (n = 8), tips for when families were at the park (n = 7), tips for when families were at appointments (n = 7), tips for when families were at the store (n = 6), and school readiness tips (n = 6).
